Let’s Make a Sandbox# We’re now going to use these commands to explore one of the most important ideas in the command line: paths.
Rather than explain paths with a diagram, let’s make a little filesystem of our own.
Start in your home directory:
cd ~You can check where you are with:
pwdNow create a directory called sandbox and enter it:
mkdir sandbox cd sandboxCheck again:
pwdYou should now be inside your new sandbox.
Let’s make some directories:
mkdir books music mkdir books/fiction books/non-fiction mkdir music/rock music/jazzAnd some files:
touch books/fiction/dune.txt touch books/non-fiction/unix.txt touch music/rock/beatles.txt touch music/jazz/miles.txtWe have now created something like this:
sandbox ├── books │ ├── fiction │ │ └── dune.txt │ └── non-fiction │ └── unix.txt └── music ├── rock │ └── beatles.txt └── jazz └── miles.txtDon’t worry if the diagram looks a little complicated. We’re going to walk around it.
Relative Paths# We are currently in:
sandboxLet’s move into books:
cd booksNow:
pwdWe’re in books.
Move into fiction:
cd fiction pwdNow let’s go back:
cd .. pwdWe are back in books.
.. means the directory above the one we’re currently in.
So from books/fiction:
cd ..takes us to:
booksWe can go up more than one level:
cd .. pwdWe’re back in sandbox.
We can also describe a route in one go.
From sandbox, try:
cd music/jazz pwdWe’ve moved into jazz.
The important thing about this path is that it is relative to where we currently are.
From sandbox:
music/jazzmeans:
Starting here, go into music, then go into jazz.
Try this:
cd .. cd ../books/fiction pwdThe path ../books/fiction means:
Go up one directory from where I am, then go into books, then fiction.
A relative path describes a route from where you are now.
Absolute Paths# There is another way to describe a location.
An absolute path describes a location starting from the root of the filesystem.
The root directory is written as:
/On a Mac, your home directory will be somewhere underneath /Users.
You can see your complete current path with:
pwdIt might look something like:
/Users/your-name/sandbox/books/fictionThat is an absolute path.
Unlike a relative path, it doesn’t matter where you currently are. The path starts at / and describes the complete route to the destination.
For example, from anywhere, you could use an absolute path to reach your sandbox:
cd /Users/your-name/sandboxOf course, you would have to replace your-name with your actual username.
An absolute path is like giving someone a complete address.
A relative path is like saying:
Go upstairs, then turn left.
The second instruction only makes sense if we know where you are starting from.
What Is ~?# Typing your entire home directory is inconvenient.
Fortunately, the shell gives us a shortcut:
~The tilde means your home directory.
So:
~/sandboxmeans:
The sandbox directory inside my home directory.
We can use it from anywhere.
Try:
cd ~Then:
pwdNow go directly back to the sandbox:
cd ~/sandboxFrom there, we can reach our music directory:
cd ~/sandbox/musicNotice that this doesn’t depend on where we started.
Let’s Wander Around# Now try navigating around the sandbox without following instructions one at a time.
Start here:
cd ~/sandboxCan you get to the Beatles file using a relative path?
cd music/rockCheck:
pwd lsYou should see:
beatles.txtNow get back to sandbox using ..:
cd ../.. pwdYou should be back in sandbox.
Can you get to the Miles Davis file using a single relative path?
cd music/jazz lsAnd now, from there, get to the Unix file:
cd ../../books/non-fiction lsFinally, use an absolute-ish path beginning with ~ to return to the fiction directory:
cd ~/sandbox/books/fiction lsThe more you do this, the less mysterious paths become.
There are two basic ways of telling the shell where something is:
absolute path "Start at the root and follow this complete route." relative path "Start where I am and follow this route."And ~ gives us a convenient name for our home directory.
You now have most of the vocabulary you need to start moving around the filesystem from the command line.
The important thing is that you don’t need to memorise a collection of commands. You need to understand what the pieces of a command mean, and know how to ask the computer when you don’t know something.

title: Process, Terminals, Shells
content:
Process# When your computer starts, the kernel is one of the first pieces of the operating system to start running. The kernel is responsible for managing the computer: its memory, CPU, devices, files and, importantly, the programs that are running.
But what does it mean for a program to be running?
From Program to Process# A program starts life as a file on a storage device. When you install an application, its code is sitting on your disk or SSD.
When you open the application, the operating system copies the parts it needs into RAM and asks the kernel to start executing its code.
That running program is a process.
So:
program on disk ↓ loaded ↓ RAM ↓ executing ↓ processYou can see this happening on a Mac without writing any code.
Open Activity Monitor. You can find it by opening Spotlight with ⌘ Space and searching for Activity Monitor.
Activity Monitor shows you the processes currently running on your computer. Some of them are applications you recognise. Many others are background processes that you have never seen before.
Leave Activity Monitor open for a moment and open another application. Watch the list. You should see new processes appear.
Close the application again. Its processes will eventually disappear.
There is much more going on here than a list of applications, though. Processes can start other processes.
PIDs# Every process has a number called a Process ID, or PID.
Look at Activity Monitor again. One of the columns is PID. This number identifies a particular process.
For example:
Application PID --------------------- Safari 3812 Calculator 4271The numbers aren’t names for the programs. They are identifiers assigned to individual processes.
We can explore this relationship more easily from the command line.
A First Look at the Command Line# For the experiments in this section, we need a way to type commands to the operating system.
On a Mac, open Terminal. You can find it with Spotlight in the same way you found Activity Monitor.
You will see a window containing something that looks roughly like this:
your-computer ~ %Don’t worry about what all of this means yet. For now, think of Terminal as a place where we can type commands and see their results. We’ll come back to exactly what a terminal and a shell are later.
Type:
pstreeand press Enter.
pstree displays processes as a tree. You may see something like:
launchd ├── Terminal │ └── zsh │ └── pstree └── ...Your output will be different. That’s fine.
Notice something interesting: pstree itself appears in the tree.
That’s because pstree is a program too. When you typed pstree, the shell started a new process to run it.
This gives us our first useful picture of processes:
shell └── pstreeThe shell is the parent and pstree is its child.
Child Processes# Processes can create other processes.
For example:
shell ├── program A └── program BHere the shell started two programs. Those programs are child processes of the shell.
A process can itself start more processes:
shell └── program A ├── worker └── workerThis is why pstree is useful. Instead of seeing processes as a flat list, we can see their relationships.
Run pstree a few times. Then open another application and run it again. Look at what changes.
The exact output will depend on your computer. The important thing is the shape of the tree.
Signals# Processes can also receive signals.
A signal is a notification sent to a process telling it that something has happened or asking it to perform some action.
For example, when you run a program in Terminal and press Ctrl-C, you are sending it a signal asking it to stop.
You can also send a signal using the process’s PID:
kill 4271Here 4271 is the PID of the process you want to signal.
Despite its name, kill does not necessarily mean “destroy this process immediately.” It is a command for sending signals to processes. Different signals have different meanings.
We’ll see more of this when we start running programs that don’t finish immediately.
Zombie Processes# There is one final oddity worth seeing.
A child process can finish running while its parent process is still alive. When this happens, the parent needs to collect some information about the child’s termination.
If the child has finished but its parent hasn’t yet collected that information, the child can temporarily appear as a zombie.
A zombie process isn’t actually running anymore. Its work is finished. What remains is a small amount of information that the operating system keeps around for its parent.
You may eventually encounter zombies when looking at process trees. Don’t confuse one with a process that is consuming CPU in the background: a zombie has already stopped running.
At this point, the important picture is:
process / \ child child / \ child childProcesses form relationships. They have PIDs so we can identify them, and they can communicate with the operating system through signals.
And, as we have just seen, even the commands we type are themselves programs that become processes when we run them.
Terminals# In the previous section, we used Terminal to run pstree.
But what exactly was Terminal?
It is tempting to think of the black window with the blinking cursor as the command line. It is actually a little more complicated than that.
A terminal is a way of interacting with a computer by typing and receiving text.
Today, a terminal is usually an application running inside our graphical desktop. In this section, we’ll see why that is the case.
A Very Short History# The story starts before computers had screens.
Early computers were large, expensive machines shared by many people. Users needed some way to communicate with them. One of the earliest solutions was essentially a typewriter connected to a computer.
You typed something. The computer received the characters. It sent characters back. The terminal printed them.
These machines were known as teletypes or teleprinters. This is where the abbreviation tty, which you may encounter later, comes from: Teletype.
The idea was simple:
computer ↕ characters ↕ terminal ↕ personThe terminal wasn’t doing the actual computing. The computer was.
Over time, paper was replaced by screens. Terminals became things like the famous DEC VT100: a keyboard and screen connected to a computer, communicating by sending and receiving characters.
Eventually, computers became small and powerful enough to sit on our desks. There was no longer much point in buying a separate physical terminal just to talk to your own computer.
So we wrote programs that pretended to be terminals.
These programs are called terminal emulators.
The terminal window you open on your Mac is one of these.
A Terminal Emulator# Open Ghostty.
Ghostty is a terminal emulator. It provides the part of the experience that an old physical terminal used to provide: a place to type characters and a place to display the characters coming back from the computer.
Ghostty itself isn’t the thing interpreting the commands you type. That’s the job of another program, called a shell, which we’ll meet in the next section.
For now, a useful mental model is:
you ↓ Ghostty ↓ shell ↓ programWhen you type something, the keystrokes travel through this system. When the program produces output, that output travels back and Ghostty displays it on your screen.
This is the basic idea behind a modern terminal.
Why Do We Still Use Terminals?# If computers have had graphical interfaces for decades, why are we still typing commands?
Because typing a command is often a very convenient way to tell a computer exactly what you want.
For example:
pstreeasks the computer to show us a process tree.
A graphical application would need to provide a button, menu or other interface for every operation it supports. A command-line program can expose the same functionality through a short command.
Terminals are particularly useful for programmers and system administrators because they make it easy to:
run programs inspect files manipulate files automate repetitive tasks install software connect to other computers That last one is particularly important.
A server in a data centre might not have a monitor, keyboard or graphical desktop at all. We can connect to it over a network and use a terminal to interact with it.
The terminal therefore isn’t just a relic from the days of giant computers. It is still one of the most useful ways of interacting with modern computers.
Some Terminals# Ghostty is the terminal we’ll use in this course. It is fast, cross-platform and designed to behave like a native application on macOS and Linux. It also supports tabs, splits and other conveniences that make working with multiple terminal sessions easier.
There are many other terminal emulators, including:
Terminal.app — Apple’s built-in terminal on macOS iTerm2 — a popular macOS terminal Kitty — a fast, feature-rich terminal Alacritty — a GPU-accelerated terminal focused on simplicity and performance They look different and have different features, but they all perform essentially the same basic job: they provide a terminal interface for programs running on your computer.
And this brings us back to processes.
When you opened Ghostty, you didn’t just open a window. You started a program. That program then started a shell, which in turn can start other programs.
We can see that entire chain in our process tree.
Ghostty └── shell └── pstreeThere are three different things here.
Ghostty is the terminal.
The shell is the program that interprets commands.
pstree** is a command that runs a program.**
We’ll look at the shell next.
Shell# In the previous section, we saw that Ghostty is a terminal. It gives us a place to type and a place to see the computer’s response.
But Ghostty isn’t actually the thing that understands what we type.
That job belongs to the shell.
Terminal ≠ Shell# When you open Ghostty, you are opening a terminal emulator. Ghostty provides the interface through which we interact with another program.
That other program is the shell.
On our machines, that shell is zsh.
The relationship looks like this:
you ↓ Ghostty ↓ zsh ↓ other programsGhostty deals with the terminal. zsh deals with the commands.
You can actually see this in our process tree:
Ghostty └── zsh └── pstreeGhostty is one process. zsh is another process running inside it. When we type pstree, zsh can start yet another process to run pstree.
The three are different things.
What Is a Shell?# A shell is a program that interprets commands.
If you’ve been following along with Sprint, this idea should feel familiar.
Sprint is essentially an interpreter. It reads an instruction, works out what that instruction means, carries it out, and then moves on to the next instruction.
A shell does something remarkably similar.
The difference is that instead of reading instructions from a map, the shell reads them from us.
We can think of its main loop like this:
print a prompt ↓ read what the user typed ↓ figure out what it means ↓ do it ↓ print a prompt ↓ read again ↓ ...In Sprint, instruction 9 means “stop”. A shell doesn’t normally reach the end after one instruction. It finishes one command and comes back asking for another.
Commands# Try this in Ghostty:
lsYou should see a list of files and directories.
What happened?
First, zsh read the characters you typed:
lsIt then worked out what ls means and ran it.
The command itself has a simple structure:
command arguments ↓ ↓ ls ...For example:
ls -l ~/DownloadsHere:
ls is the command name -l is an argument ~/Downloads is another argument Arguments give the command additional information about what we want it to do.
This is somewhat like the instructions in Sprint.
In Sprint:
1 10 20 30The 1 tells us what operation to perform, while the other numbers provide information needed by that operation.
A shell command has a similar idea:
ls -l ~/Downloadsls tells the shell which command we want, while the remaining pieces provide information to that command.
Does the Shell Do Everything?# Not quite.
This is one of the most important things to understand about a shell.
Some commands are built into the shell itself. Others are separate programs that the shell starts.
Try:
pwdThen:
lsBoth look like commands. But they don’t necessarily work in the same way.
ls is a separate program. When zsh encounters it, zsh finds the program and starts it as a new process.
We can see this happening with pstree.
Run:
pstreeYou’ll see something resembling:
Ghostty └── zsh └── pstreeThe pstree process exists while the command is running. When it finishes, that process disappears.
The shell remains.
Ghostty └── zshThis is the difference between the shell interpreting a command and the shell launching another program.
Built-in Commands# Some commands need to be handled by the shell itself.
Try:
cd ..cd means “change directory.”
This cannot simply be handled by starting another program.
Why?
Because the shell itself needs to change its current directory.
Imagine zsh did this:
zsh └── cdThe cd program could change its directory and then finish. But zsh would still be sitting in its original directory.
Instead, cd is built into the shell. zsh handles it itself.
This gives us two broad categories:
command │ ┌─────────┴─────────┐ ↓ ↓ shell handles it shell launches another process │ │ cd lsThis distinction is useful because a shell is not simply a collection of programs. It is itself a program that understands some commands and knows how to launch other programs.
Many Shells# zsh is not the only shell.
There are many different shells, just as there are many different terminal emulators.
Some you may encounter are:
zsh — the shell we use Bash — one of the most widely used shells fish — designed to be particularly friendly and interactive sh — a very old and influential shell They all serve the same basic purpose: they interpret commands and provide a way for us to interact with the operating system.
They differ in their features, syntax and behaviour.
For our purposes, we’ll use zsh.
Back to Sprint# There is a useful way to think about everything we’ve seen so far.
Sprint takes instructions and interprets them:
instruction ↓ Sprint ↓ operationA shell takes commands and interprets them:
command ↓ zsh ↓ operation or another processBut there is one enormous difference.
Sprint’s instructions were designed specifically for Sprint. We wrote the interpreter and defined what instructions like 1, 3, 5 and 9 meant.
A shell lives in a much bigger world.
Its commands can cause the operating system to perform useful work, and many of those commands are actually separate programs.
So when you type:
ls -l ~/Downloadsyou aren’t asking Ghostty to list some files.
You’re typing characters into a terminal. Ghostty passes those characters to zsh. zsh interprets them, finds the ls program, and starts a new process with the arguments -l and ~/Downloads.
you ↓ Ghostty ↓ zsh ↓ ls -l ~/Downloads ↓ ls process ↓ output ↓ zsh ↓ GhosttyThe terminal gives us the window.
The shell understands our commands.
The processes do the work.

title: More Recursion
content:
A Few More Loops to Avoid# Liked the recursion problems?
Here are a few more.
Same rules as before: try to solve each problem by making the problem smaller, and let the function call itself.
Two Ways to Recur# There are two common ways we will write recursive functions.
They do the same sort of work, but they keep track of things differently.
1. The Accumulator# Sometimes we pass the answer-so-far as an argument.
For example, suppose we want to add all the numbers from 1 to x:
f(x, total) = total when x = 0 = f(x - 1, total + x)We might start with:
f(3, 0)which becomes:
f(3, 0) → f(2, 3) → f(1, 5) → f(0, 6) → 6The total argument carries our partial answer through the recursion.
2. The Smaller Answer# The other approach is perhaps more familiar.
Instead of carrying the answer-so-far, we ask the smaller problem for its answer:
f(x) = 0 when x = 0 = x + f(x - 1)So:
f(3) → 3 + f(2) → 3 + (2 + f(1)) → 3 + (2 + (1 + f(0))) → 6Here, the answer is built as the recursive calls return.
No Global Variables# There is another important idea hiding here.
When writing functions in this mathematical style, we don’t declare some global variable and quietly change it as the function runs.
If a recursive function needs to remember something, pass it as an argument.
That is why the accumulator version has total as a parameter.
The information a function needs should be visible in its arguments.
Two styles. Same recursion. Different places to keep the information.
1. Digit by Digit# Write a recursive function that calculates the sum of the digits of a positive integer.
For example:
f(7) = 7 f(12) = 3 f(123) = 6 f(501) = 6Think about how you can separate the last digit from the rest of the number.
2. How Many?# Write a recursive function that calculates the number of digits in a positive integer.
f(7) = 1 f(42) = 2 f(1234) = 4What is the smallest number you can solve immediately?
What happens to the number when you remove one digit?
3. Power Trip# Write a recursive function that calculates (x^n).
For example:
power(2,1) = 2 power(2,2) = 4 power(2,3) = 8 power(3,4) = 81Remember that:
$$ x^n = x \times x^{n-1} $$
So the recursive part is practically writing itself.
Almost.
4. Division, Revisited# Earlier, you calculated the remainder of a division.
Now calculate the quotient.
Write a recursive function that calculates how many times y can be subtracted from x before x becomes smaller than y.
For example:
quotient(10,3) = 3 quotient(5,3) = 1 quotient(12,4) = 3You may find it useful to think of:
10 → 7 → 4 → 1as three subtractions.
What should the function return when x < y?
5. Letter Counter# Write a recursive function that counts how many times a particular letter occurs in a word.
For example:
count("hello", "l") = 2 count("banana", "a") = 3 count("hello", "z") = 0You already have functions for getting the first letter of a word and everything after it.
You will also need to decide whether two letters are the same.
You could define a small helper function:
same(x,y) = true when x and y are the same letter = false otherwiseThen ask:
How many times does x occur in this word?
The answer depends on whether the first letter is x, and how many times x occurs in the rest of the word.
6. Palindrome Patrol# A palindrome is a word that reads the same forwards and backwards.
For example:
"level" "radar" "racecar"Write a recursive function that determines whether a word is a palindrome.
For example:
palindrome("level") = true palindrome("hello") = false palindrome("a") = true palindrome("") = trueYou may want to define some helper functions first:
first(x) = first letter of x last(x) = last letter of x middle(x) = everything except the first and last letters of xYou already know how to get the first letter and remove the first letter.
Can you build last and middle from those?
Then the real question becomes:
Are the first and last letters the same, and is everything in between also a palindrome?
That’s recursion hiding in plain sight.

title: More Functions in Math
content:
Functions — Beyond the Basics# From mathematical functions to programming functions# 1. Where We Are# We already know that a function:
Takes some input Applies a rule Produces an output Has a domain and a range For example:
f(x) = 2x + 3If we give it 5:
f(5) = 2(5) + 3 = 13So far, we have mostly treated functions as rules for transforming values.
Now we will ask:
What else can we do with functions?
2. Functions Can Be Combined# Suppose we have two functions:
f(x) = 2x g(x) = x + 3We can apply one function after another.
First g, then f:
f(g(x))Substitute:
f(g(x)) = f(x + 3) = 2(x + 3) = 2x + 6This is called function composition.
3. Function Composition# Composition can be written as:
(f ∘ g)(x) = f(g(x))Read this as:
“f composed with g”
The important idea is the order:
x → g → f → resultFor example:
g(x) = x + 3 f(x) = 2x (f ∘ g)(x) = f(g(x)) = 2(x + 3) = 2x + 6 4. Composition Is Not Usually Commutative# With ordinary multiplication:
2 × 3 = 3 × 2But function composition generally does not work this way.
Consider:
f(x) = 2x g(x) = x + 3Then:
(f ∘ g)(x) = f(g(x)) = 2x + 6But:
(g ∘ f)(x) = g(f(x)) = 2x + 3Therefore:
f ∘ g ≠ g ∘ fThe order in which functions are applied matters.
5. Composition as a Pipeline# We can think of composition as a pipeline.
x ↓ g ↓ g(x) ↓ f ↓ f(g(x))For example:
x = 5 g(x) = x + 3 f(x) = 2xThe pipeline is:
5 → 8 → 16This idea becomes extremely important in programming.
A program can be thought of as a collection of transformations:
input → transformation → transformation → transformation → output 6. The Identity Function# There is a special function that does nothing to its input.
I(x) = xThis is called the identity function.
For any function f:
f(I(x)) = f(x)and:
I(f(x)) = f(x)Therefore:
f ∘ I = I ∘ f = fThe identity function is analogous to the number 0 for addition or 1 for multiplication: it leaves something unchanged.
7. Inverse Functions# What if a function transforms a value and we want to reverse the transformation?
Consider:
f(x) = x + 5If:
f(3) = 8we can reverse the operation by subtracting 5.
Define:
f⁻¹(x) = x - 5Then:
f⁻¹(8) = 3So:
3 → f → 8 → f⁻¹ → 3An inverse function undoes what the original function does.
8. Inverses and Composition# If f⁻¹ is truly the inverse of f, composing them should give us the identity function.
f⁻¹(f(x)) = xand:
f(f⁻¹(x)) = xFor example:
f(x) = 2x + 3 f⁻¹(x) = (x - 3) / 2Check:
f⁻¹(f(x)) = f⁻¹(2x + 3) = ((2x + 3) - 3) / 2 = xThis connects three ideas:
function ↓ inverse ↓ composition ↓ identity 9. Not Every Function Has an Inverse# Consider:
f(x) = x²We have:
f(2) = 4 f(-2) = 4Two different inputs produce the same output.
If we are given 4, we don’t know whether the original input was:
2or:
-2Therefore, there is no unique inverse function over all real numbers.
This leads us to an important property of functions.
10. One-to-One Functions# A function is one-to-one if different inputs always produce different outputs.
For example:
f(x) = 2x + 1Some values:
f(1) = 3 f(2) = 5 f(3) = 7 f(4) = 9No two inputs give the same output.
A one-to-one function is also called injective.
Informally:
One input → one unique output and no two inputs share an output.
11. Injective, Surjective, Bijective# Consider a function:
f : A → BThere are three useful properties.
Injective# Different inputs have different outputs.
a₁ ≠ a₂ ⇒ f(a₁) ≠ f(a₂)Surjective# Every element of B is reached by at least one element of A.
Bijective# A function is both injective and surjective.
A bijective function gives a perfect one-to-one correspondence between the two sets.
12. Why Bijections Matter# Consider:
A = {1, 2, 3} B = {a, b, c}A bijection could be:
1 → a 2 → b 3 → cEvery element in A maps to exactly one element in B.
And every element in B is reached.
Because the mapping is one-to-one and onto, it can be reversed:
a → 1 b → 2 c → 3The inverse exists because there is no ambiguity.
13. Piecewise Functions# A function does not have to use the same rule everywhere.
For example:
f(x) = x² if x ≥ 0 -x if x < 0Different parts of the domain use different rules.
Evaluate:
f(3) = 3² = 9But:
f(-3) = -(-3) = 3This is a piecewise-defined function.
14. Piecewise Functions and Absolute Value# A familiar example is the absolute value function.
|x| = x if x ≥ 0 -x if x < 0So:
|5| = 5 |-5| = 5Piecewise functions are useful because they show that:
A function is defined by its mapping, not necessarily by one simple formula.
15. Piecewise Functions in Programming# A piecewise function is very close to conditional logic.
Mathematically:
f(x) = x² if x ≥ 0 -x if x < 0Conceptually:
if x >= 0: return x² else: return -xThe programming language is simply giving us another way to express the same mathematical idea.
16. Functions Can Be Treated as Objects# So far, our functions have taken values as inputs.
For example:
f(x) = x²But what if the input itself is a function?
Consider:
F(f, x) = f(x) + 1Now f is itself an input.
If:
f(x) = x²then:
F(f, 3) = f(3) + 1 = 9 + 1 = 10The function F has received another function as an argument.
17. Functions Can Produce Functions# A function can also return another function.
Consider:
F(a) = a function that adds aMore formally:
F(a)(x) = x + aFor example:
F(5)(x) = x + 5So:
F(5)(3) = 8The first application gives us a new function:
F(5)The second application gives us a value:
F(5)(3) 18. Higher-Order Functions# A higher-order function is a function that:
takes one or more functions as arguments, or returns a function. For example:
H(f, x) = f(x)²If:
f(x) = x + 1then:
H(f, 3) = f(3)² = 4² = 16Here, H receives a function as an input.
19. A Function That Modifies Functions# Consider:
f(x) = x²We could define:
addOne(f)(x) = f(x) + 1Then:
addOne(f)(3) = f(3) + 1 = 9 + 1 = 10But notice what happened.
We started with:
f(x) = x²and created a new function:
g(x) = x² + 1So a function can transform another function into a new function.
20. Functions Are Values# This gives us a powerful general principle:
Functions can be treated like values.
A value can be:
stored passed around given as an argument returned from another operationAnd so can a function.
For example:
number → value string → value function → valueThis is one of the conceptual foundations of functional programming.
21. Anonymous Functions# Sometimes we need a function only temporarily.
Instead of naming it:
f(x) = x²we can simply describe the function itself:
x ↦ x²This is an anonymous function: a function without a permanent name.
For example, suppose we want to apply:
x ↦ x²to:
5The result is:
5² = 25Programming languages often provide special syntax for these unnamed functions.
22. Functions Over Different Kinds of Values# Mathematical functions don’t have to map numbers to numbers.
For example:
length : Strings → Natural NumbersA possible mapping is:
length("hello") = 5 length("cat") = 3 length("functions") = 9Or:
uppercase : Strings → StringsFor example:
uppercase("hello") = "HELLO"The idea of a function is much more general than:
number → number 23. Functions Over Collections# We can also have functions that operate on collections.
For example:
sum : Lists of Numbers → NumbersThen:
sum([1, 2, 3, 4]) = 10Or:
length([10, 20, 30]) = 3Or a function that transforms every element:
square([1, 2, 3, 4]) = [1, 4, 9, 16]This is where mathematical functions begin to look very much like programming functions.
24. Mapping# Suppose:
f(x) = x²We can apply f to every element of a collection:
[1, 2, 3, 4]giving:
[1², 2², 3², 4²]which becomes:
[1, 4, 9, 16]This operation is commonly called map.
Conceptually:
map(f, [x₁, x₂, ..., xₙ]) = [f(x₁), f(x₂), ..., f(xₙ)]The important part is that map receives a function as input.
25. Filtering# Another useful operation is filtering.
Suppose:
p(x) = "x is even"Given:
[1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]we can keep only the values for which p is true:
[2, 4, 6]Conceptually:
filter(p, [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]) = [2, 4, 6]Again, the operation receives a function.
This is another example of a higher-order function.
26. Currying# Consider a function with two parameters:
f(x, y) = x + yNormally we provide both values at once:
f(2, 3) = 5Currying changes the way we think about this function.
Instead of:
f(x, y)we can think of it as:
f(x)(y)The first function receives x and returns another function waiting for y.
27. Currying Step by Step# Consider:
add(x, y) = x + yA curried version can be thought of as:
add(x)(y) = x + yNow:
add(5)doesn’t produce a number.
It produces a new function:
g(y) = 5 + yThen:
g(3) = 8Therefore:
add(5)(3) = 8Currying makes functions that return functions especially explicit.
28. Partial Application# Currying naturally leads to partial application.
Start with:
multiply(x, y) = x × yFix the first argument:
multiplyBy10(y) = 10 × yNow we have created a specialized function.
For example:
multiplyBy10(3) = 30 multiplyBy10(7) = 70We started with a general function:
multiply(x, y)and created a more specific function:
multiplyBy10(y) 29. Recursion# A function can call itself.
This is called recursion.
Consider factorial:
n! = n × (n - 1)!For example:
5! = 5 × 4! = 5 × 4 × 3! = 5 × 4 × 3 × 2! = 5 × 4 × 3 × 2 × 1!Eventually we need a stopping point.
0! = 1This is called the base case.
30. The Structure of a Recursive Function# A recursive definition generally has two parts:
Base case# The condition where recursion stops.
f(0) = some known valueRecursive case# The function defines itself in terms of a smaller version of the same problem.
f(n) = some expression involving f(n - 1)For factorial:
factorial(0) = 1 factorial(n) = n × factorial(n - 1)Without the base case, the function would never stop.
31. Tracing Recursion# Consider:
factorial(4)The recursive expansion is:
factorial(4) = 4 × factorial(3) = 4 × 3 × factorial(2) = 4 × 3 × 2 × factorial(1) = 4 × 3 × 2 × 1 × factorial(0) = 4 × 3 × 2 × 1 × 1 = 24Notice that recursion doesn’t mean:
“Do something infinitely.”
It means:
“Reduce the problem until we reach a case we already know how to solve.”
32. Recursion on Sequences# Functions over integers are particularly useful for recursion.
Consider:
a(0) = 1 a(n) = 2a(n - 1)Then:
a(0) = 1 a(1) = 2 a(2) = 4 a(3) = 8 a(4) = 16This is a recurrence relation.
A recurrence defines a value in terms of previous values.
33. Fibonacci# The Fibonacci sequence is another famous recursive definition.
F(0) = 0 F(1) = 1 F(n) = F(n - 1) + F(n - 2)Therefore:
F(0) = 0 F(1) = 1 F(2) = 1 F(3) = 2 F(4) = 3 F(5) = 5 F(6) = 8The mathematical definition is already extremely close to a recursive program.
34. Functions as Transformations# There is another useful way to think about a function.
Instead of thinking:
“A function is an equation.”
Think:
“A function is a transformation between sets.”
For example:
f : A → Bmeans:
f maps elements from set A to elements of set B.
For example:
f : Integers → Integers f(x) = x + 1The function transforms:
... -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, ...into:
... -1, 0, 1, 2, 3, ... 35. Functions Are More General Than Equations# Consider:
f(x) = x²This is a convenient way of describing a function.
But a function can also be represented as:
A table# x f(x) 1 1 2 4 3 9 4 16A graph# Each input corresponds to exactly one output.A rule# Square the input.A mapping# 1 → 1 2 → 4 3 → 9 4 → 16The function is the underlying relationship, not the particular representation.
36. Function Transformations# Starting with:
f(x) = x²we can create related functions.
Vertical shift:
g(x) = f(x) + 3Horizontal shift:
g(x) = f(x - 3)Vertical scaling:
g(x) = 2f(x)Horizontal scaling:
g(x) = f(2x)These expressions show that functions themselves can be transformed.
37. Operations on Functions# Functions can participate in operations just like numbers.
Suppose:
f(x) = x² g(x) = x + 1We can define:
(f + g)(x) = f(x) + g(x)Therefore:
(f + g)(x) = x² + x + 1Similarly:
(f - g)(x) = f(x) - g(x)and:
(fg)(x) = f(x)g(x)and:
(f / g)(x) = f(x) / g(x)where the division is defined.
38. Composition Is Another Operation on Functions# We can now see composition differently.
If:
f(x) = 2x g(x) = x + 3then:
(f ∘ g)(x) = f(g(x))So there are operations that combine functions:
f + g f - g fg f / g f ∘ gThe result is often another function.
39. Properties of Functions# Functions can have interesting properties beyond their formulas.
For example:
Even# f(-x) = f(x)Example:
f(x) = x²Odd# f(-x) = -f(x)Example:
f(x) = x³Periodic# There is some positive T such that:
f(x + T) = f(x)Example:
sin(x + 2π) = sin(x)These properties describe behaviour, not merely the formula.
40. Increasing and Decreasing Functions# A function can also describe a trend.
If increasing x generally increases f(x), the function is increasing.
For example:
f(x) = 2x + 1As x increases:
x: 1 2 3 4 f(x): 3 5 7 9The outputs increase.
Other functions may decrease, or may increase in some regions and decrease in others.
41. Functions Can Have Different Domains# The same expression can define different functions depending on its domain.
Consider:
f(x) = x²Over the real numbers:
f : ℝ → ℝBut we could instead define:
f : ℤ → ℤNow the function only accepts integers.
Or:
f : {1, 2, 3} → ℝNow it accepts only three possible inputs.
The domain is not an afterthought.
The domain is part of the function.
42. Functions in Programming# We can now reinterpret a programming function mathematically.
A function such as:
double(x)might represent:
double(x) = 2xA function such as:
square(x)might represent:
square(x) = x²And a function such as:
compose(f, g)might represent:
compose(f, g)(x) = f(g(x))Programming gives us a way to execute these mathematical transformations.
43. The Important Shift in Thinking# Initially, we think:
function = formulaBut a more powerful understanding is:
function = transformationThen:
function ↓ can be composed ↓ can be inverted ↓ can be passed around ↓ can be returned ↓ can transform other functions ↓ can be applied recursivelyThis is the bridge from elementary mathematics to programming.
44. One Big Example# Suppose:
f(x) = x² g(x) = x + 1We can compose them:
h(x) = f(g(x)) = (x + 1)²We can then transform h:
k(x) = h(x) + 5So:
k(x) = (x + 1)² + 5We could also define a function that takes h itself:
addFive(h)(x) = h(x) + 5Then:
addFive(h)(3) = h(3) + 5 = 16 + 5 = 21We are no longer just calculating with functions.
We are calculating with functions themselves.
45. From Values to Functions# There are several levels of abstraction.
Level 1 — Values# x = 5Level 2 — Functions producing values# f(x) = x²Level 3 — Functions taking functions# H(f, x) = f(x) + 1Level 4 — Functions producing functions# F(a)(x) = x + aLevel 5 — Functions transforming functions# transform(f)(x) = f(x) + 1This is a major conceptual transition toward functional programming.
46. A Mental Model for Programming# When you encounter a programming function, ask:
What are its inputs?# domainWhat does it produce?# rangeWhat transformation does it perform?# mappingCan it be composed with another function?# f(g(x))Can it receive another function?# H(f, x)Can it return another function?# F(x)(y)Can it call itself?# f(x) → f(smaller problem)These questions turn programming functions into something mathematically familiar.
47. Summary# We began with:
input → function → outputWe can now extend that model:
input ↓ function ↓ outputFunctions can also:
compose with other functionsbe invertedtake functions as inputsreturn functions as outputsbe transformed into other functionsoperate on collectionsbe defined recursively 48. The Big Idea# A function is not merely:
f(x) = some formulaA function is a mapping or transformation.
And once we accept that functions are things we can manipulate, we can build increasingly powerful ideas:
Functions ↓ Composition ↓ Inverse functions ↓ Functions as values ↓ Higher-order functions ↓ Anonymous functions ↓ Currying / partial application ↓ Recursion ↓ Functional programmingThe mathematical concept stays the same.
What changes is what we are willing to do with functions.

title: Functions in Math
content:
Functions — A Little Bit of Function# 1. What Is a Function?# A function is a rule that takes an input and produces an output.
For example:
f(x) = 2x + 3Give it 5:
f(5) = 2(5) + 3 = 13So we can think of a function as:
input → function → output 2. Evaluating Functions# If:
f(x) = x² + 1then:
f(2) = 2² + 1 = 5The x is simply replaced by the input.
Similarly:
f(3) = 10 f(4) = 17 f(5) = 26The expression f(x) describes the function.
The expression f(3) means we have applied the function to 3.
3. Functions Can Take Functions’ Outputs# Suppose:
f(x) = 2x g(x) = x + 3We can put the output of one function into another:
f(g(x))First calculate g(x):
g(x) = x + 3Then apply f:
f(g(x)) = f(x + 3) = 2(x + 3) = 2x + 6This is called composition.
We write:
(f ∘ g)(x) = f(g(x))Think:
x → g → f → result 4. Order Matters# With the same functions:
f(x) = 2x g(x) = x + 3we have:
f(g(x)) = 2x + 6But:
g(f(x)) = 2x + 3Therefore:
f(g(x)) ≠ g(f(x))In general, function composition is not commutative.
The order in which we apply functions matters.
5. Functions Can Have More Than One Input# A function need not have just one input.
For example:
f(x, y) = x + yThen:
f(2, 3) = 5Or:
g(x, y) = xygives:
g(4, 5) = 20The basic idea remains:
inputs → function → output 6. Functions as Mappings# There is another way to think about a function.
Suppose:
f(x) = x²We could write:
1 → 1 2 → 4 3 → 9 4 → 16Or as a table:
x f(x) 1 1 2 4 3 9 4 16The formula is one way of describing the function.
The table is another.
The important thing is the mapping:
input → output 7. One Input, One Output# There is one rule that must always hold:
Every input must have exactly one output.
For example:
1 → 2 2 → 4 3 → 6is a function.
But:
1 → 2 1 → 5is not.
The input 1 has two different outputs.
Different inputs may have the same output, however:
1 → 5 2 → 5 3 → 7is perfectly valid.
8. Domain and Range# The domain is the set of possible inputs.
The range is the set of outputs produced.
For example:
f(x) = x²If the domain is:
{1, 2, 3}then:
1 → 1 2 → 4 3 → 9and the range is:
{1, 4, 9}The domain is part of the definition of a function.
9. Functions Can Be Used to Define Functions# Suppose:
f(x) = x²We can define another function using f:
g(x) = f(x) + 1Therefore:
g(3) = f(3) + 1 = 9 + 1 = 10We can also compose several functions:
h(x) = f(g(x))Functions can therefore be built from other functions.
10. One Last Thing# There is a useful distinction to keep in mind.
fis a function.
f(5)is the result of applying that function to 5.
If:
f(x) = 2x + 1then:
f(5) = 11So:
function ≠ result of applying the functionThis distinction will become increasingly useful.
11. Where Next?# We began with:
input → function → outputBut functions can do more than simply turn numbers into other numbers.
They can be:
composed combined invertedand, perhaps more interestingly, functions themselves can be inputs and outputs.
There is quite a lot more to functions than f(x) = ....

title: Math Recursion
content:
Recur and Tear# A small collection of exercises for getting comfortable with recursive functions, base cases, reducing problems to smaller problems, and the occasional mathematical ambush.
1. Even Steven# Write a recursive function that adds all the even numbers between 0 and x.
If x is even, include x in the result.
For example:
f(3) = 2 f(4) = 6 f(5) = 6 f(10) = 30Your function should work for any non-negative integer x.
2. Odd One Out# Write a recursive function that adds all the odd numbers between 0 and x.
For example:
f(1) = 1 f(2) = 1 f(3) = 4 f(5) = 9 f(7) = 16 f(9) = 25As before, the function should work for any non-negative integer x.
The trick is not to calculate the entire sum from scratch every time.
3. A String of Events# Now let’s leave numbers behind.
All arguments to f,g,h, and cat are words. A word is a sequence of zero or more letters.
Consider:
f(x) = "" when x is "" = first letter of xSo:
f("hello") = "h" f("ab") = "a" f("") = ""We also have:
g(x) = "" when x is "" = all but the first letter of xSo:
g("hello") = "ello" g("ab") = "b" g("") = ""And finally:
cat(x,y) = join x and yFor example:
cat("he","llo") = "hello" cat("","a") = "a"Now consider:
h(x) = "" when x is "" = cat(h(g(x)),f(x))Evaluate:
h("hello")Be careful.
There is recursion here, but there is also a small change happening to the argument each time.
4. A Little Left Over# Division can be thought of as repeatedly taking away the divisor.
For example, when calculating:
10 ÷ 3we can take away 3 three times:
10 → 7 → 4 → 1There is nothing more to take away.
The number left over is 1.
Write a recursive function that calculates the remainder of a division.
For example:
modulo(10,3) = 1 modulo(5,3) = 2Your function should work for positive integers.
The Recursive Recipe# For each of the functions above, you should be able to answer three questions:
What is the base case? How does the problem get smaller? How does the answer to the smaller problem help produce the answer to the original problem? If you cannot answer all three, your function probably isn’t recursive yet.
It is merely thinking about being recursive.
And thinking about recursion is not recursion.
Shun the loops. Embrace the smaller problem.

1. A Simple Sum# Evaluate:
f(x) = x + 2 g(x) = 3x f(2) + g(3)2. In n Out# Evaluate:
f(x) = 3x g(x) = x - 2 f(g(2))3. Karthik Calling Karthik# Evaluate:

9. Dis order# Give an example of two functions f and g such that:

Think carefully about the domain of each function before answering.
11. Lunatic calendar# Write a function that calculates the number of days in a month, given the number of the month from 0 to 11.

12. The Plot Thickens# Consider:

h(5)Pay attention to the difference between a function and the result of calling a function.
Shunning the func ain’t the same as function

title: Designing Logic Gates
content:
The Million-Dollar Warehouse# There is an old warehouse on the outskirts of Bangalore. According to the records you found, the warehouse contains a fortune large enough to completely change your life.
There is one problem: the owners knew exactly how valuable the contents were.
To protect the warehouse, they decided to install a highly secure automated entrance system. You have been given the responsibility of designing the logic that controls the entrance.
The entrance is used by employees to access a restricted area. The door remains locked whenever the security system is not active.
During normal operation, an employee can enter when their access has been authorized. Authorization can be established by presenting a valid access card. A security guard at the entrance may also approve the employee’s entry.
The warehouse also has an emergency lockdown feature. When lockdown is activated, the door must remain closed, even if an employee would otherwise be authorized to enter.
Your Task# Design the logic for the automated entrance system based on the requirements above.
Your submission should contain:
The input and output variables, with a clear definition of each. Truth table — Construct the complete truth table for your Boolean expression. The Boolean expression for the entrance system. The logic-gate diagram implementing the Boolean expression. Example# Suppose the requirement is:
A security alarm should activate when the system is armed and a door is open. The alarm should remain inactive when the system is in maintenance mode.
Inputs
A — System is armed D — Door is open M — System is in maintenance mode Output
Y — Alarm is active Truth Table
Construct the complete truth table to verify your expression and circuit. Boolean Expression
Y = A · D · ¬M (or) Y = A AND D AND (complement of M) ¬M means complement of M Logic Diagram
Represent the Boolean expression using the appropriate AND and NOT gates.

title: Logic
content:
Logic: The Machinery of Reasoning# You already know more logic than you think.
Every time you say:
“If it is raining, I should carry an umbrella.”
or:
“I will have tea if there is milk and sugar.”
or:
“I will go out if it is Saturday or Sunday.”
you are using logic.
You don’t need a computer, a formula, or a mathematics degree to use it. Logic is simply a way of describing how statements combine and how we reason from one statement to another.
We have already covered the mechanics of Boolean logic in class. This post is a chance to step back and look at the bigger picture: what logic is, why it is useful, and why the same ideas keep appearing in apparently unrelated parts of mathematics.
1. Logic is about true and false# Let’s start with some ordinary statements:
It is raining. The shop is open. Today is Monday. I have a ticket. 7 is an even number.Each of these can be classified as true or false.
For example:
"7 is an even number."is simply false.
Logic gives us a way to take statements like these and combine them into larger statements.
Suppose:
A = It is raining. B = I am carrying an umbrella.Then:
A AND Bmeans:
It is raining and I am carrying an umbrella.
Similarly:
A OR Bmeans:
It is raining or I am carrying an umbrella.
And:
NOT Ameans:
It is not raining.
This is the basic idea behind Boolean logic.
2. Why is this called Boolean logic?# The name comes from George Boole, a 19th-century English mathematician.
Boole was interested in a rather ambitious question:
Can reasoning itself be expressed using mathematics?
In 1854, he published An Investigation of the Laws of Thought, developing a system in which statements could be manipulated using mathematical rules.
He wasn’t thinking about Python, computers, or mobile phones. None of those things existed.
Yet his system turned out to be extraordinarily useful for computers.
Why?
Because computers ultimately have to distinguish between two states. A circuit can be on or off. A switch can be open or closed. A bit can be 1 or 0.
So we can associate:
TRUE ↔ 1 FALSE ↔ 0And suddenly the mathematics of reasoning becomes useful for building machines.
This is one of the fun things about mathematics:
You don’t always know what an idea will eventually be useful for.
3. A tiny language for reasoning# The basic logical operations you have already seen give us a remarkably small language.
Suppose:
A = It is raining. B = I have an umbrella.We can make statements such as:
NOT A A AND B A OR B A XOR BThe first three are probably familiar.
XOR is slightly more particular. It means one or the other, but not both.
For example:
A = I am having tea. B = I am having coffee.Then:
A XOR Bmeans:
I am having either tea or coffee, but not both.
The important thing is that we can build bigger statements from these small pieces.
For example:
A = It is raining. B = I have an umbrella. C = I am going outside. C AND (A AND B)means:
I am going outside, it is raining, and I have an umbrella.
We are taking ordinary sentences and treating them almost like building blocks.
4. Logic is also algebra# This is where Boolean logic starts becoming interesting.
In ordinary algebra, you can manipulate expressions without changing what they mean.
For example:
2 × (3 + 4)can be rewritten as:
(2 × 3) + (2 × 4)Boolean logic has its own rules for doing something similar.
One of the most famous examples is De Morgan’s theorem:
NOT (A AND B) = (NOT A) OR (NOT B) NOT (A OR B) = (NOT A) AND (NOT B)The notation may look intimidating, but the idea is quite natural.
Imagine:
A = It is raining. B = It is cold.Consider:
It is not true that it is raining and cold.
For that to be true, at least one of the two things must fail:
It is not raining or it is not cold.
So:
NOT (raining AND cold)is equivalent to:
NOT raining OR NOT coldHere’s another everyday example.
Suppose I say:
I am not having both tea and coffee.
That means:
I am not having tea or I am not having coffee.
Notice how the AND became an OR, and the NOT moved inside.
That’s De Morgan’s theorem in ordinary language.
5. Statements can talk about other statements# So far, we have mostly been combining statements.
Formal logic goes one step further and lets us talk about relationships between statements.
Consider:
If it is raining, then the ground is wet.
Let’s give the two parts names:
A = It is raining. B = The ground is wet.Then we can write:
A → Bwhich means:
If A is true, then B is true.
This is called a conditional.
We use conditionals constantly in ordinary life:
If I am hungry, I will eat. If the shop is closed, I will come back tomorrow. If today is Sunday, I don't have to go to work. If a number is divisible by 4, it is even.The interesting thing is that once we have a conditional, we can transform it in several different ways.
6. The family of conditional statements# Start with a simple statement:
If it is raining, then the ground is wet.
Let’s call the two parts:
A = It is raining. B = The ground is wet.Our original statement is therefore:
A → BThere are three particularly important ways of transforming this statement.
6.1 The converse# The converse swaps the two parts:
If the ground is wet, then it is raining.
In symbols:
A → B B → AThis sounds reasonable at first, but it is not necessarily true.
The ground could be wet because someone watered the garden.
So the converse is related to the original statement, but it is not generally equivalent to it.
6.2 The inverse# The inverse negates both parts:
If it is not raining, then the ground is not wet.
In symbols:
A → B NOT A → NOT BAgain, this is not necessarily true.
It could be sunny while the garden is being watered.
So:
If it is not raining, the ground is not wet.
doesn’t follow from:
If it is raining, the ground is wet.
6.3 The contrapositive# The contrapositive does two things:
Swap the two parts. Negate both of them. Starting with:
If it is raining, then the ground is wet.
we get:
If the ground is not wet, then it is not raining.
In symbols:
A → B NOT B → NOT AAnd this one is special:
A statement and its contrapositive are logically equivalent.
If the original statement is true, its contrapositive must be true, and vice versa.
7. The four forms side by side# It is useful to see the whole family together.
Starting with:
If it is raining, then the ground is wet.
we get:
Form Statement Equivalent to original? Conditional If it is raining, the ground is wet. — Converse If the ground is wet, it is raining. ❌ Inverse If it is not raining, the ground is not wet. ❌ Contrapositive If the ground is not wet, it is not raining. ✅ There is a useful relationship hiding here:
Conditional → Contrapositive ↕ ↕ Converse → InverseThe conditional and contrapositive are equivalent.
The converse and inverse are also equivalent to each other.
But neither pair is generally equivalent to the other.
So, if:
A → Bis true, we automatically know:
NOT B → NOT Ais true.
But we cannot automatically conclude:
B → Aor:
NOT A → NOT Bare true.
This distinction is worth remembering because reversing a statement is not the same thing as taking its contrapositive.
8. A mathematical example# Consider:
If a number is divisible by 4, then it is even.
Let:
A = The number is divisible by 4. B = The number is even.The four forms are:
Conditional
If a number is divisible by 4, it is even.
Converse
If a number is even, it is divisible by 4.
Not true. 6 is even, but it isn’t divisible by 4.
Inverse
If a number is not divisible by 4, it is not even.
Also not true. 6 isn’t divisible by 4, but it is even.
Contrapositive
If a number is not even, it is not divisible by 4.
True.
Notice how useful the contrapositive can be. Sometimes proving or understanding:
If A, then B
is easier by thinking about:
If NOT B, then NOT A.
9. Logic and sets are surprisingly similar# Now let’s leave statements for a moment and look at sets.
Suppose we have a group of people who like tea and a group of people who like coffee.
A = people who like tea B = people who like coffeeWhat does the intersection mean?
A ∩ BIt means:
People who like tea AND coffee.
What does the union mean?
A ∪ BIt means:
People who like tea OR coffee.
This is not merely a convenient analogy.
The correspondence is exact.
For any person x:
x ∈ A ∩ Bmeans:
x is in A AND x is in B.
And:
x ∈ A ∪ Bmeans:
x is in A OR x is in B.
We can think of it like this:
flowchart LR A["People who like tea"] --> I["Intersection ∩"] B["People who like coffee"] --> I I --> R["Like tea AND coffee"] A2["People who like tea"] --> U["Union ∪"] B2["People who like coffee"] --> U U --> R2["Like tea OR coffee"]There is another correspondence too.
The complement of a set means:
Everything that is not in the set.
That is very similar to NOT in logic.
So we have:
Logic Sets AND ∩ OR ∪ NOT ComplementDifferent objects, different notation, but remarkably similar rules.
10. The same idea keeps appearing# This is one of the most important things to notice about mathematics.
Mathematics is not just a giant collection of unrelated topics.
Very often, different mathematical systems describe the same underlying structure.
Consider:
Boolean logic Set theory Digital circuits ProgrammingThey look like completely different subjects.
But all of them can contain versions of:
AND OR NOTFor example:
Logic Sets Programming AND Intersection ∩ and OR Union ∪ or NOT Complement not The symbols aren’t really the important part.
The important thing is that the relationships between the operations are the same.
Once you start noticing this, mathematics becomes a little less like memorising hundreds of separate rules.
You start asking:
“Is this actually the same idea I’ve seen somewhere else?”
Quite often, the answer is yes.
11. Different mathematical worlds can describe the same thing# Here’s an even stranger idea.
Suppose you want to describe the number 3.
You could simply write:
3But mathematics gives us many other ways to construct objects.
For example, we could describe numbers using sets. We could describe operations using functions. We could describe relationships using logic.
In principle, entire branches of mathematics can be constructed from more fundamental systems.
This means that the usual picture we have of mathematics:
Numbers Geometry Algebra Calculus Logic Sets Probability ...as a collection of separate subjects is somewhat misleading.
There are deep connections between them.
You can sometimes take one system and build another system on top of it.
For example, arithmetic can be developed from logical and set-theoretic foundations.
And the connection goes in the other direction too: logic itself can be implemented using physical systems such as digital circuits.
So we get a rather beautiful map of connections:
flowchart TD L["Logic"] --> S["Sets"] S --> N["Numbers"] N --> A["Arithmetic"] L --> C["Computation"] C --> P["Programs"] L --> D["Digital circuits"]This shouldn’t be interpreted as a strict hierarchy where one subject is simply “more fundamental” than another.
It is better thought of as a map of connections.
The same ideas can be expressed in different languages.
12. Why should you care?# At this point you might reasonably ask:
“Okay, but why are we talking about this?”
There are two reasons.
First: logic is everywhere.# Whenever you have to decide whether something is true, or whether several conditions are simultaneously true, you are doing logic.
Is it raining? Is the shop open? Do I have enough money? Is the number even?And when you combine those questions:
It is raining AND I have an umbrella. The shop is open OR it is Saturday. The number is NOT even.you are doing Boolean logic.
Second: recognising the structure is more useful than memorising the rules.# You don’t want to become someone who has memorised a list of Boolean identities but doesn’t recognise when they are useful.
You want to be able to look at something unfamiliar and think:
“Hang on. This looks like AND and OR.”
That is a much more powerful skill.
13. And eventually, programming# You have only just started programming, so you don’t need to know how deeply logic connects to computer science yet.
For now, just notice the obvious connection.
The things you have been writing:
if x > 10: ...and:
if raining and carrying_umbrella: ...are logical statements.
When your programs become more complicated, you will spend a surprising amount of time expressing conditions clearly:
if age >= 18 and has_ticket: ...The programming language gives you a convenient syntax, but underneath it is still the same basic machinery:
TRUE FALSE AND OR NOTThe computer isn’t doing something fundamentally different from the logic we have been discussing.
It is simply very, very good at it.
14. Exercises# The best way to get comfortable with logic is to play with it.
Exercise 1 — Everyday logic# Write each of these using AND, OR, and NOT.
a.
I will go for a walk if it is not raining.
b.
I will have dessert if I have finished dinner and there is some left.
c.
I will watch a movie if it is Friday or Saturday.
Try giving names to the individual statements first.
Exercise 2 — De Morgan’s theorem# Rewrite these without an outer NOT:
NOT (It is raining AND it is cold)NOT (I have a ticket OR I have a pass)Say the resulting statements out loud. If they sound strange, that’s fine. The point is to convince yourself that the two versions mean the same thing.
Exercise 3 — The four forms# Start with:
If it is raining, then the ground is wet.
Write down:
The conditional The converse The inverse The contrapositive Then identify which ones are logically equivalent.
Try the same exercise with:
If a number is divisible by 10, then it is divisible by 5.
Exercise 4 — Tea and coffee# Suppose:
A = people who like tea B = people who like coffeeExplain in plain English what each of these means:
A ∩ B A ∪ B AᶜNow invent your own two sets and do the same thing.
Exercise 5 — Find logic around you# For one day, pay attention to statements containing words such as:
and or not if unless either bothWrite down five examples.
Then try translating each one into a logical expression.
You will probably discover that people use logic constantly without ever calling it logic.
The big idea# Don’t worry about memorising every symbol or terminology you encountered in this post.
The important idea is much simpler:
Logic gives us a language for talking precisely about what is true, what is false, and how the truth of one statement relates to another.
And once you learn to recognise that structure, you start seeing it everywhere.
In ordinary language:
It is raining AND I have an umbrella.In sets:
A ∩ BIn programming:
a and bIn digital electronics:
AND gateThese are not four completely unrelated ideas.
They are four different ways of expressing a remarkably similar idea.
That is perhaps the most useful lesson to take away from logic:
the symbols may change, the terminology may change, and even the subject may change—but the underlying structure can remain the same.
Further Rabbit Holes# If this post has made you even slightly curious about logic, there are some wonderfully strange places you can go next.
You don’t need to study these topics systematically. Pick one that sounds interesting and follow the rabbit hole.
People worth knowing# George Boole# The obvious place to start.
Boole developed the algebra of logic that we now call Boolean algebra—long before computers existed.
If you want to understand where the AND, OR, and NOT you use in programming ultimately come from, start with George Boole.
Lewis Carroll# Yes, that Lewis Carroll—the author of Alice’s Adventures in Wonderland.
Carroll was also deeply interested in logic and wrote books and puzzles about it. His logical puzzles are a delightful reminder that formal reasoning doesn’t have to look like a mathematics textbook.
Look for:
Lewis Carroll’s logic puzzles Carroll’s syllogisms Symbolic Logic It’s particularly amusing to discover that the person who wrote about the Mad Hatter and the Cheshire Cat was also spending his time thinking about formal reasoning.
Bertrand Russell# Russell was one of the great logicians and philosophers of the early 20th century.
He is particularly famous for Russell’s Paradox, which begins with a deceptively innocent question:
What happens if we consider the set of all sets that do not contain themselves?
That tiny question caused serious problems for attempts to build all of mathematics from set theory.
A more accessible version is the Barber Paradox:
A barber shaves everyone in the village who does not shave themselves. Does the barber shave himself?
Try answering it before looking up the solution.
Kurt Gödel# Gödel took the question of mathematical logic much further.
His incompleteness theorems showed, roughly speaking, that sufficiently powerful formal mathematical systems contain statements that are true but cannot be proved using the rules of that system.
That’s an astonishing result.
If you enjoy questions like:
“Can mathematics prove everything that is true?”
then Kurt Gödel is your rabbit hole.
Alan Turing# Turing connects logic directly to computing.
Before modern computers existed, Turing described an extremely simple theoretical machine that could perform computations. These Turing machines became one of the foundations of theoretical computer science.
Even more interesting is the halting problem:
Can we write a program that looks at any other program and determines whether that program will eventually stop?
The answer is no.
This is a wonderful example of logic telling us something fundamental about computers—not merely how to build them, but what computers can and cannot do.
Raymond Smullyan# If the historical figures sound a little intimidating, try Raymond Smullyan.
Smullyan wrote numerous books turning formal logic into puzzles, games, riddles, and detective problems.
A particularly famous family of puzzles is Knights and Knaves:
Knights always tell the truth. Knaves always lie. You meet some people. They make statements. You have to work out who is who. These puzzles are an excellent way to practice logical reasoning without feeling like you’re doing mathematics.
Paradoxes worth exploring# Paradoxes are particularly good introductions to logic because they start with questions that sound completely reasonable and then lead somewhere very strange.
The Liar Paradox# Consider:
This statement is false.
If the statement is true, then it is false.
If it is false, then it is true.
So… what is going on?
This is one of the oldest and most famous examples of self-reference causing trouble.
Russell’s Paradox# This is the mathematical cousin of the Liar Paradox.
Very roughly:
Consider the set of all sets that do not contain themselves.
Now ask:
Does that set contain itself?
If it does, then by its definition it shouldn’t.
If it doesn’t, then by its definition it should.
The question seems almost silly. Its consequences were anything but silly.
Search for Russell’s Paradox if you want to see how a seemingly harmless idea about sets helped shake the foundations of mathematics.
Zeno’s Paradoxes# Zeno of Elea came up with several paradoxes involving motion.
The most famous involves Achilles and the tortoise.
Suppose a tortoise gets a head start in a race. Before Achilles can catch the tortoise, he must reach the point where the tortoise was. But by then the tortoise has moved a little further. Achilles reaches that point, but the tortoise has moved again.
So does Achilles ever catch the tortoise?
Of course he does.
But explaining exactly why the argument appears to suggest otherwise leads into some fascinating ideas about infinity, limits, and calculus.
The Monty Hall Problem# This one is especially fun because your intuition will probably tell you one thing while probability tells you another.
You are shown three doors:
Door 1 Door 2 Door 3 🚗 🐐 🐐Behind one is a car. Behind the other two are goats.
You choose a door.
The host, who knows where the car is, opens one of the other doors and reveals a goat.
You are then given a choice:
Stay with your original door, or switch to the remaining unopened door?
Should you switch?
Don’t look up the answer immediately. Work it out first.
Search for Monty Hall Problem when you’re ready to see why the answer is surprising.
The Unexpected Hanging Paradox# A judge tells a prisoner:
“You will be executed next week, but the execution will be a surprise.”
The prisoner reasons about which day the execution can occur and apparently manages to conclude that it cannot happen at all.
And yet, when the execution happens, it is still a surprise.
This is a particularly nice example of reasoning about what someone knows about what someone else knows.
Search for Unexpected Hanging Paradox or Surprise Examination Paradox.
Logic puzzles# If you would rather do logic than read about it, look for:
Knights and Knaves# As mentioned above, these are Raymond Smullyan’s classic truth-teller/liar puzzles.
They are probably the closest thing to a logic workout disguised as a game.
The Hardest Logic Puzzle Ever# This is a famous puzzle by George Boolos involving three gods:
one always tells the truth, one always lies, one answers randomly. You have to determine who is who.
There are additional complications involving the fact that the gods speak a language in which you don’t know which word means “yes” and which means “no.”
It is spectacularly over-engineered.
It is also a wonderful demonstration of just how much information can be packed into carefully constructed questions.
Logic puzzle books by Raymond Smullyan# If the Knights and Knaves puzzles appeal to you, Smullyan has plenty more.
Look for:
What Is the Name of This Book? The Riddle of Scheherazade Alice in Puzzle-Land The last one is especially appropriate if the Lewis Carroll connection interests you.
Logic and computers# There is a natural progression from the logic you’ve just learned to computer science.
Start with logic gates.
An AND gate is essentially:
A AND BAn OR gate is:
A OR BA NOT gate is:
NOT ACombine enough of these simple components and you can build increasingly complicated digital circuits.
Eventually you can build things capable of performing arithmetic and computation.
That gives you a beautiful connection:
Logic ↓ Logic gates ↓ Digital circuits ↓ Computers Turing machines# Then look at Turing machines.
Don’t be put off by the name. The basic idea is remarkably simple: imagine a machine that reads symbols from a tape, follows a small set of rules, and changes the symbols on the tape.
That’s it.
From this almost ridiculously simple setup, Turing was able to investigate what it means for something to be computable.
The Halting Problem# Once you know a little programming, try this question:
Can you write a program that can look at any program and tell you whether that program will eventually finish or run forever?
It sounds like something a sufficiently clever programmer should be able to do.
It turns out that no such general program can exist.
This is the Halting Problem, and it is one of the great results connecting logic with computer science.
It is worth thinking about before reading the proof.
And finally: Gödel, Escher, Bach# If you want to go much further down the rabbit hole, there is Douglas Hofstadter’s Gödel, Escher, Bach.
It brings together:
logic mathematics computation music art recursion self-reference consciousness It is not an easy book, and you absolutely do not need to read it for this course.
But it is a fascinating example of what happens when you start looking for the same patterns across completely different subjects.
And that, ultimately, is what this entire post has been trying to get you to notice.
A possible path# If you don’t know where to begin, try this:
George Boole ↓ Boolean logic ↓ Lewis Carroll ↓ Logic puzzles ↓ Bertrand Russell ↓ Paradoxes ↓ Kurt Gödel ↓ Alan Turing ↓ The Halting ProblemOr, if you prefer puzzles to history:
Knights and Knaves ↓ Monty Hall Problem ↓ The Liar Paradox ↓ Russell's Paradox ↓ The Hardest Logic Puzzle EverYou don’t need to follow either path to the end.
Pick whichever question makes you curious enough to search for the answer. That’s usually the best way to learn.

title: The Missing Diamond
content:
🔎 The Missing Diamond# The Case# At 8:00 PM, the famous Blue Star Diamond disappeared from a locked display room at the City Museum.
There were only three people inside the museum at the time:
Arun — Security Guard
Meera — Museum Assistant
Ravi — Electrician
The police arrived immediately.
The display room had no broken windows or damaged locks.
🕵️ Clue 1 — The Security Camera# The camera showed that the display room was opened at 7:42 PM.
The museum assistant, Meera, had the access card needed to open the room.
But there was one problem:
The access card was used while Meera was standing in the cafeteria.
So, did Meera steal the diamond?
🔦 Clue 2 — The Power Cut# At 7:40 PM, the museum experienced a short power failure.
The electrician, Ravi, was working near the electrical control room.
The security guard said:
“During the power cut, I went downstairs to check the main switch.”
So both Ravi and Arun had a reason to be near the electrical room.
But the diamond could only be removed if:
The display room was opened and the security alarm was disabled.
🧩 Clue 3 — The Alarm# Police discovered that the alarm was disabled at 7:41 PM.
Only Arun’s security code could disable it.
However…
Arun’s code was entered from inside the security office.
And Arun’s fingerprint was not found on the security-office keyboard.
☕ Clue 4 — The Unexpected Detail# A coffee cup was found beside the security-office computer.
It had Meera’s fingerprint on it.
Meera immediately said:
“Yes, I had coffee there earlier. But I didn’t enter the security code.”
The investigators now had three possibilities.
